* fix: run a query against its own environment's project

`run_show_with_manager` selected `root_project_dir` as the prepared
invocation's project, falling back to `cwd`. `root_project_dir` is not
the selected project: `worktree::handlers::query_paths` builds it as the

checkout's `.env`, and anchored the target/index paths there, while the
child's cwd stayed the worktree — compiling against the main checkout's
models and macros instead of the environment's edits. For the default
environment `cwd == root_project_dir`, so the defect was invisible
there.

Select `cwd`. `root_project_dir` keeps the two roles it has everywhere
else in this file: a fallback for locating the dbt binary/venv
(`resolve_dbt_for_query`) and a second entry in the profile search order
(`profiles_dir_for_resolve`).

The existing test pinned the defect — it passed a worktree as `cwd`, a
different directory as `root_project_dir`, and asserted `--project-dir`
and the `.env` of that other directory. It now pins the contract: when
`cwd != root_project_dir` the child gets `--project-dir <cwd>`, the
worktree's `.env`, the worktree as its cwd, and no trace of the source
checkout.

* fix(dbt-index): commit a rebuilt index only once every table is written

The index writers loop over the ~39 tables and stop at the first error.
Each file was renamed into place as soon as it was written, so a failure
partway through left the tables before it updated and the ones after it
stale, with no single write that produced the mix on disk. Any other
process that imports the directory sees that mix.

Writing now stages every table to a temp path and commits them together
once all have succeeded. A staged table that is never committed deletes its
temp file on drop, including the one whose write failed, so a failed attempt
leaves neither a half-updated index nor leftover temp files.

Staging uses `.parquet.staging.tmp`. The hydration and serve writers use the
plain `.parquet.tmp` for individual tables in the same directory, and a
staged index write holds its temp files for the whole write rather than one
table, so sharing the name would let the two truncate each other. The suffix
is not digits, so the legacy layer sweeper still leaves it alone.

The merge modes read their own table's destination file, so deferring the
renames does not change what any of them see.

This is not full atomicity: a rename that fails, or a crash between renames,
still leaves a mix. Closing that needs a directory swap or a pointer file.
The streaming IndexWriter used by the Fusion path has the same property and
is left for a follow-up.

### Problem

On Fusion, source tests and singular tests never get a top-level `group`, even when you set `config.group`. Core 1.x copies that config onto `group`. Selectors like `group:…`, `state:modified`, and group notifications all look at the top-level field, so those tests quietly drop out of group-based workflows.

Generic tests on models are already fine — they inherit the parent model's group, and we should leave that alone (including the case where the parent has no group).

If the test has no `attached_node`, use `config.group`. If it does (model/seed/snapshot), keep inheriting the parent.

* fix: align dbt State materialization classification with the python plugin

* fix: align dbt State materialization classification with the python plugin

Fusion and the dbt State python plugin classified materializations by
different rules, so the same node could be submitted under a different
execution type depending on which engine built the request.

Port python's `utils.py` predicates verbatim into a new
`dbt-state::materialization` module and use them at every run-cache
decision point. They classify by materialization *name* rather than by
`DbtMaterialization` variant because Fusion has no variant for every
name python knows — `semantic_view` parses as `Unknown`.

Behavior changes, all toward python:

- `materialized_view` submits as VIEW instead of FULL, so it takes the
  cheap view path (own last_modified plus query hash, no dependency
  traversal) as it does in python.
- `dynamic_table`, `metric_view`, `streaming_table`, `interactive_table`
  and `external` submit as DBT_CUSTOM instead of FULL. They are still
  submitted and can still be skipped, but DBT_CUSTOM is not in the
  server's cloneable execution types, so they are no longer offered as
  clone candidates — cloning cannot soundly reproduce a dynamic table
  with its own refresh schedule.
- `semantic_view` is no longer submitted at all; python's `is_table` and
  `is_view` both reject it.
- A full-refreshed snapshot submits as FULL instead of SNAPSHOT, and an
  incremental model with a custom strategy stays DBT_CUSTOM under
  `--full-refresh`. python gates the whole incremental/snapshot branch on
  full refresh and decides DBT_CUSTOM ahead of it.

`is_custom_materialization` takes the union of both definitions rather
than replacing Fusion's: python classifies by name, while Fusion resolves
which macro dbt would actually dispatch, which additionally catches a user
macro shadowing a built-in name such as `table` (dbt-core#14486).

* chore: describe materialization rules without naming the reference client

Code under fs/sa/ is published externally, so comments there must not
narrate another implementation's source layout. Restate the
classification rules, branch ordering and submit gate on their own terms
and drop the file/line citations. No behavior change.

* fix: keep shadowed views and inline models out of the wrong classification

Two issues raised in review, both consequences of combining the
name-based and dispatch-based classifications.

A user macro shadowing `view` or `materialized_view` made `is_view` and
`is_custom_materialization` true at the same time, which the name-only
check could never produce. The execution type is derived by checking
`is_view` first, so those models kept the view fast path: reuse decided
on the target's own freshness and query hash, with no dependency
traversal, even though the dispatched macro runs user code that may not
produce a view at all. Give custom precedence by excluding shadowed
names from `model_is_view`, and share that helper with the two submit
paths that previously classified view-ness on their own.

The table classification is exclusion-based, so `inline` — which has no
warehouse relation at all — fell through as a table and was reported in
state-explain output as both ephemeral and a table. Exclude no-op
materializations from that field.

Regression tests cover a shadowed `view` and `materialized_view`, and an
inline model's explain info.

* fix: apply the custom-materialization fallbacks to adapter-specific names

Review follow-ups.

`node_uses_custom_materialization` still asked only the dispatch-based
resolver, which reports adapter-internal macros as built-in. Routing
`metric_view` off the view path sends it through dependency collection
for the first time, and its compiled code is not necessarily SQL, so an
empty or unparseable body would skip the manifest fallback or propagate
the parse error and leave freshness dependencies incomplete. Reuse the
same name-plus-dispatch union the submitted execution type uses, so the
fallbacks and the wire classification agree on what custom means.

Also rename the name-based predicate to `is_custom_by_name`, since
`is_custom_materialization` already names the dispatch-based check on
`MaterializationResolver`, and route the execution-type derivation
through the shared incremental-strategy normalizer instead of repeating
the `+` stripping inline.

* fix: keep the microbatch event-time filter on relations derived from a ref

* fix: keep the microbatch event-time filter on relations derived from a ref

Closes #16392

Resolves dbt-labs/dbt-core#16383

### Problem

In a microbatch model, a relation derived from a ref, such as `{{ ref('x').include(...) }}`, drops the batch's event-time filter, so each batch reads the whole upstream table while the delete only covers the batch window. dbt Core keeps the filter.

`RelationObject::call_method` re-wraps the derived relation with `RelationObject::new`, which resets `run_filter` and `event_time`.

### Solution

`include`, `quote`, `replace_path`, `incorporate` and `without_identifier` now re-wrap through a helper that keeps the filter, matching dbt v1. `derivative`, `create_from` and `information_schema` point at a different object and are unchanged.

Tested with a `jinja_assert` test covering all five (it fails without the fix) and end to end on Snowflake, running microbatch models over a 2-day window of a 10-day source:

| Model reads | 2.0.6 | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `ref('src')` | 2 rows | 2 rows |
| `ref('src').include(database=false)` | 19 rows | 2 rows |
| `ref('src').quote(...)` | 19 rows | 2 rows |
| `ref('src').replace_path(identifier=...)` | 19 rows | 2 rows |
| `ref('src').incorporate(path=...)` | 19 rows | 2 rows |

`without_identifier()` has no table to read, so it is covered by the unit test only.

Resolves dbt-labs/dbt-core#16477

### Problem

When a unit test overrides a package-qualified macro in `overrides.macros`, such as `my_project.is_ci`, every other macro in that package becomes undefined, and the test fails with `value of type undefined is not callable`. dbt-core replaces only the overridden macro.

`bind_override_macros` in `crates/dbt-tasks-sa/src/renderable/renderable/unit_test.rs` puts a one-entry map with the stub in front of the package namespace, using `ObjectOverlay`. As the issue explains, that map answers every other name with undefined. The overlay also never asks the package namespace, which resolves macros only through `get_property`.

Reproduced on DuckDB with the macros and model from the issue (`pick_label()` calls `my_project.is_ci()`), both in the root project and with the project installed as a package through `local: ..`:

| Unit test | dbt 2.0.6 / 2.0.7 | dbt-core 1.12.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| overrides `my_project.is_ci: true`, expects `ci` | error | pass |
| overrides `my_project.unused_macro: "stub"`, expects `local` | error | pass |
| no override, expects `local` | pass | pass |

### Solution

- `ObjectOverlay` skips undefined values, as the issue suggests, so the stub no longer answers names it does not define.
- It also forwards `get_property` to its layers in order. Package namespaces resolve their macros there, not in `get_value`, so skipping undefined values alone still fails, with `unknown method: map has no method named pick_label`.
- Macros called through the package still see the override: `pick_label()` gets the stubbed `is_ci` and returns `ci`, as in dbt-core.

Tested with `cargo nextest run -p dbt-tasks-sa` (new tests: `test_package_macro_override_is_seen_by_other_package_macros`, `test_package_macro_override_keeps_unrelated_package_macros`). The tests use a small namespace that, like `DbtNamespace`, resolves macros only through `get_property`, since `DbtNamespace` is not reachable from `dbt-tasks-sa` without adding a dependency. With a local build, all three unit tests pass in both setups.

This does not change the error location the issue also reports.

### Problem

All `modules.re` top-level functions (`compile`, `match`, `search`, `fullmatch`, `findall`, `split`, `sub`) silently ignored keyword arguments (`flags=`, `maxsplit=`, `count=`). When a function like `re.findall(pattern, s, flags=re.DOTALL)` was called, the kwargs were silently dropped, meaning `(.*)` wouldn't match across newlines, causing empty results for downstream macros.

This impacts macros relying on the `re` module with keyword arguments, including the dbt-clickhouse `materialized_view` materialization.

### Solution

All `modules.re` functions have been updated to use `ArgsIter` (which is already used for `Capture::call_method` in the same file) to correctly extract both positional arguments and trailing kwargs (like `flags=`, `maxsplit=`, `count=`).

Additionally, the execution paths for `Pattern::call_method` and the top-level free functions were split. This ensures compiled pattern methods enforce their Python-equivalent signature (e.g., `Pattern.findall` does not take `flags` as they are already baked into the compiled pattern).

Closes #16457

Resolves dbt-labs/dbt-core#16476

Port of databricks/dbt-databricks#1688

### Problem

With `use_materialization_v2` off (the default), when a Databricks view model replaces an existing table or other non-view relation, the view materialization drops the existing relation first and only then creates the view. If the view fails to build, the run fails and the table is already gone.

### Solution

Route that case through `get_replace_sql`, the replacement flow the V2 view path already uses. The view is created at the `__dbt_stg` staging relation first, then swapped in, so a failed build leaves the existing table in place. V1 and V2 now replace a relation of a different type the same way. View-over-view runs keep the existing `create or replace view` path, and grants and tags are applied in the same order as before.

The V1 branch of the vendored `view.sql` matches #1688 byte for byte. The replace-flow macros it calls (`get_replace_sql`, `create_backup`, `execute_multiple_statements`) are already vendored and match current dbt-databricks.

The `dbt-loader` view materialization test for an existing Databricks table now asserts that the first statement creates the view at the staging relation and that the table is renamed out of the way. It fails on `main`, where the view is created directly at the target after the drop.

Took a Claude stab at resolving #16418

### Problem

Users using v2 are unable to use Jinja filters where the attribute arg is an integer. See example in #16418

### Solution

The `map` filter already handled both kinds of argument correctly. I reused its approach rather than writing a new one:

1. **Read `attribute` as any value**, not only a string.
2. **Look it up based on its type** with a shared helper, `get_attr`:
   - a string is looked up by name or dotted path, as before (`"name"`, `"a.0"`)
   - anything else, like an integer, is looked up by position (`0`, `1`)
3. **Use a second helper, `get_attr_or_default`,** for filters that fall back to a default when the lookup fails or finds nothing. It replaces the old `get_path_or_default`, which only took strings; I removed that since nothing uses it any more.

* fix(dbt-agate): #15412 convert Arrow FixedSizeList instead of panicking

Snowflake delivers `VECTOR(FLOAT, n)` to the driver as Arrow
`FixedSizeList(Float32, n)`. Reading such a column into an agate table panicked:

    CastError("Casting from FixedSizeList(.., 1024) to Utf8 not supported")

Two things had to line up for this. `flat_record_batch.rs` forwards
`FixedSizeList` as a flat column rather than expanding it, so it does reach the
conversion phase; and `make_array_converter` had arms for `List`, `LargeList`,
`Map` and `Struct` but not `FixedSizeList`, so it fell through to the `_ =>`
fallback that unconditionally casts to `Utf8`. Arrow has no such cast kernel, so
the returned `CastError` was unwrapped by `AgateTable::new` into a panic.

This makes `FixedSizeList` render as a Jinja sequence, like the other list
converters. Because a fixed-size list has no offsets buffer, the child range for
row `idx` is computed from `value_length`; `FixedSizeListArray::slice()` already
re-slices the child, so no extra offset term is needed (covered by a test).

Tracking issue #3947 listed `FixedSizeList` under "not doing" on the premise
that nested types are always flattened before conversion. The flattener
contradicts that for this type, and Snowflake `VECTOR` is the case that hits it.

Impact: one `VECTOR` column anywhere in the changed set aborted the entire
Advanced CI "compare changes" step.

Note: the issue also suggests replacing the `unwrap()` in `AgateTable::new` with
a named error. That turns a widely-used constructor into a fallible API across
~22 caller files in dbt-adapter, dbt-tasks-sa, dbt-loader and sdf-adapter, so it
is left to a follow-up rather than bundled here.

CVE-2026-94266.d12746f32acca82af22fe736a99827f2f0b15a91:
Supply git credentials through a credential helper instead of the clone URL (#16862) (#16865)

* Supply git credentials through a credential helper instead of the clone URL

libcurl 7.81.0-1ubuntu1.30 (CVE-2026-94266) strips credentials from
CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL. git uses it to follow redirects, so a clone whose URL
embeds credentials and whose repository URL redirects loses them on the
follow-up request and fails with 'could not read Username ... expected flush
after ref listing'. dbt deps passes the rendered package URL, credentials
included, straight to git clone.

Split http(s) credentials out of the URL and supply them through a git
credential helper configured with GIT_CONFIG_* env vars, scoped to the
repository's origin. git only calls a helper after a 401, like URL credentials,
so public repositories with a placeholder token behave as before (an
Authorization header would not: it is sent up front and GitHub rejects an
invalid one). The credentials stay out of argv, the logged command and the
clone's .git/config. Applied to clone, sparse-checkout and fetch.

Resolves #16861



* Keep credentials out of git error messages and shorten comments

GitCloningError, GitCheckoutError, UnknownGitCloningProblemError and the
'never saw Cloning into' error still interpolated the original URL, token
included. Use the credential-free URL, and pass the auth env to run_cmd
directly instead of falling back to None at each call site.



* Assert the credential given to git, not the clone URL, in secret scrubbing test

* Upgrade Jinja2 dependency version specification to address CVE-2024-22195 (#9638)

CVE-2024-22195 identified an issue in Jinja2 versions <= 3.1.2. As such
we've gone and changed our dependency requirement specification to be
3.1.3 or greater (but less than 4).

Note: Preivously we were using the `~=` version specifier. However due
to some issues with the `~=` we've moved to using `>=` in combination
with `<`. This gives us the same range that `~=` gave us, but avoids
a pip resolution issue when multiple packages in an environment use `~=`
for the same dependency.
